facts.text: The path from the old road to the lower lake is overgrown but cairned across the talus; fallen trees at each end of the talus make it easy to lose. Above the upper lake expect a brush bash to reach the talus gully, in both directions.
In early August snow can still cover the ground above about 5,600 ft; a short, moderately steep snow fin near 6,300 ft is the one place an axe is welcome.
Poles and microspikes for the snow above 5,600 ft (early August)

In mid-May snow becomes continuous from about 4,500 ft, burying the boulder fields so that legs punch through the gaps; a short class 3 step near 4,800 ft above the upper lake leads to snow slopes that run to a notch around 5,800 ft.
In late May the lower lake can still be mostly frozen, and the ridge narrows to a snow fin near 6,400 ft; the summit area itself is bare.
In mid-October the boulder fields are bare with open gaps between blocks, and the cairns above the lakes point in conflicting directions.
A day trip by bike should be off the rough, cobbled road before dark; riding it at night caused crashes.

facts.text: In early June the Dingford and Myrtle Lake trail is clear except thin snow patches near the lake, but side streams run high.
The gully up to Big Snow Lake is dry until a waterfall near its top that runs hard in early June; exit climber's left by a steep dirt ramp around 4,800 ft to stay off the wet rock.
In early June snow is continuous from Big Snow Lake to the summit and soft enough that crampons stayed in the pack; the descent can be plunge-stepped or glissaded.
In early July the snow above the lakes was hard and steep with poor runouts, so an axe is essential and crampons were wished for; mosquitoes and gnats swarm the Myrtle Lake camps.
Going up through the boulder field and then turning right onto the ridge beats the second waterfall chute, which has crumbly rock.
Dropping straight down the fall line below the Big Snow Lake outlet lands in extremely thick brush; keep to the north side of the bowl for lighter bushwhacking.
The narrow gully directly above Snowflake Lake has a short steep stretch of loose kitty-litter rock; the main gully farther west is longer but easier.
In a dry September the route was snow-free and axes stayed packed, but extra brush and route-finding made the day longer.
